blocks.x: Lead us still there. Here comes it. We're ready now. Okay.
Okay. What's the day?
Today is August 2th. Okay, 1978. Right. And we're at the same place, Bernard Amstano's house. Right, right. Okay. Called Bernie. Yeah. Well, I happened to find something in Esquire's Jazz Book 45.
It was just a notation I made about Oscar Marcour.
Mm-hmm.
And it didn't say a great deal more, except that I didn't remember what he played, if I ever really knew.
Yeah, you may not have mentioned it to me.
Yeah, I don't think he did. I heard him live once, by the way. Oh, really? The New Orleans Jazz Club.
Huh.

Yeah. But he, you know, he said that he knew and he'd played with people like the Halfway House Orchestra, New Orleans Jazz Club. And that he thought Emmett Hardy was better than Dix. And that he'd made at least one side privately. But then all sorts of other people have said the same sort of thing.

Yeah. Well, it's nice to have confirmation. Instead of something, say, coming from my faith all along. And also I found a napkin signed by some people from the Italian Village at 115 Columbus Avenue, San Francisco.

Oh, yeah, that was, the Italian Village was a nightclub down more or less near the North Beach area in San Francisco. And for some years, the Turk Murphy Band worked in the, I think, least and worked in the lower level of the place. They had a, you know, standard nightclub and show and restaurant up above. And the, the Murphy Band worked below. And this was at least from 1952, and I suspect a little bit earlier, until they got into the earthquake lagoon business a number of years later. When I was an intern in San Francisco at Southern Pacific General Hospital, which later on became, and quite recently, the Harkness Pavilion, my wife and I went down to the Italian Village not long after we'd gotten there. And Patty being more forward than I, didn't require being very forward, introduced herself and me to Turk. And we became really quite friendly with the band, particularly with Turk and with Bob Short and his wife of that particular period. And visited, did some visiting back and forth throughout the years. At that time, well, the band was composed of Turk, Murphy on trombone, Bob Short on cornet, Bob Helm clarinet, Wally Rose Piano, and Dick Lemie on string bass and tuba. And they played a lot of good stuff. They, a lot of Oliver Armstrong and Morton tunes, but also they had a lot of interest in a number of old tunes, including Burt Wheeler material, some show tunes, and some more or less obscure things. I think Turk, or one of the guys in the band, were the people that dug up the Triangle Jazz Blues, and maybe the only people who've recorded it, at least they were the first. One thing they were very scrupulous with was keeping track of what they played, I assume, to pay royalties on it, which a lot of bands didn't do.
Hmm. Who was Burt Wheeler?
Burt Wheeler?
Isn't that the name I'm trying to think of?
This was the, uh, the great black entertainer from the, uh...
Williams. Burt Wheeler. Yeah.
Yeah, I was thinking of Wheeler and Williams, which was his partner, wasn't it? I don't know.
There was a Burt Wheeler who was a comedian in the movies, I thought.
Oh, that was not, okay. A white guy. That was a white guy. No, Burt Williams. Yeah.
And what was the business of Earthquake and Williams? How did that work?

I'm not quite sure how that happened. My understanding was that the, uh, was that Turk and, uh, Pete Kloot, his piano player for a number of years now, and either all or some, or maybe none of the other guys in the band, bought this building sort of on the edge of Chinatown and turned it into a, uh, club called Earthquake Magoons where the Murphy band was entertainment. Uh, it was popular for a number of years. I hear it's been sold now. Oh, this is, this is quite recently. Uh, they added a kind of a mildly interesting thing in the, in the cellar, uh, several years ago called The Magic Cellar, which, uh, around which there's an interesting story. I don't know if it belongs in there or not, because it doesn't have anything to do with jazz. But, uh, I'll ramble on for a minute. Uh, Turk says that Turk has been involved with all sorts of hobbies, but he's been involved in, in, in old cars, in sports cars for, for many years. And, uh, Pete Clute also was, and they had a couple of cars stored in a barn somewhere on the peninsula. And they were notified they were going to have to move it as a barn was being sold, or move it. And they went over there to talk to the people, apparently. And they said there was some kind of a, an estate being settled, and the place and its contents were to be auctioned off. And they poked around some and found a number of large packing cases, uh, which turned out to be the elaborate props of a very prominent magician of the 1920 period, I believe. He had been on tour in India and apparently had died suddenly in India, and all of the props, tricks, and all sorts of stuff had been shipped back and stored since then, around 1930. And, uh, they were, they had apparently had some kind of passing interest in magic, or suddenly developed one, or knew people who did. And they went to the auction and bid it in and got a vast array of some very elaborate magical paraphernalia. Uh-huh. And they had a second or third basement in Earthquake Magoon, which they turned into the, into the magic cellar, which I went to a couple of times with my wife, Barbara. and, uh, it was a fascinating, my, my interest in magic is very slight, but it was a fascinating stuff, because a lot of the things were obviously 1920, 1930 vintage, and were, were done very attractively and elaborately. Uh-huh. It was, it was kind of an interesting place.

I really don't know enough about Turk Murphy to ask you. You know, I've heard the rackets, and I've heard him a lot, but not that often. They ask you much more, unless you can think of something else.

Well, one thing that I found of interest was, was, his difficulty in speaking. Turk has, since I first met him, a stammer, particularly if he's speaking to strangers, but also if he's speaking to people he knows. But he doesn't, I've never heard him stammer once when he sings. And he does vocals quite frequently. And I'm not sure what that signifies, but I've heard some, something like that stated of another, of another musician. I wonder if it has some, I'm sure it has some kind of significance, but I don't know what. I think that's a well-known medical fact. One of many. One of many.

And I think, I think I came across it in some comedy routine, maybe in a book, some humorous part of a book. Anyway, back to New Orleans, if we may. I think I interrupted you and got off the subject. We were talking about coming down on weekends from Baton Rouge, maybe a couple of days or now.
Yeah.
How did that work?

I was, I was 20 and 21, and I'm finishing my pre-med studies. And my family was in New Orleans. And I would try very hard, both to catch Roger Wolfe's jazz show on WDSU, which I think was on Friday nights, may have been Saturdays. And also, sometimes, to go to jazz club meetings. Because the New Orleans jazz club, I think, started in 47. Might have been 46, but it was around that time. There were a couple of abortive initial attempts. And also, to go to the Parisian Room concerts, which were down in the 100 block of Royal Street, in the building that, in a quite old building that had housed Gluck's, that was currently, at least at the time, housing Gluck's Restaurant and some other places. And the Parisian Room was a hall upstairs. And I remember some of the first people I heard there. Most particularly, I remember Irving Fazola, who was the one I'd heard most of. But a number of other musicians, including Sharky, Lester Bouchon, Chink Martin, Monk Hazel, Frank Federico. Those are the ones that come to mind. I'm particularly impressed with Fazola. who died, I think, within a year or two of that.

I think he died in 49. That was before, he died before I came to New Orleans in 49. In any case, but he'd been around for many, many years and in and out of town, of course, too. So he had a reputation. Yeah,
he'd been with Bob Crosby.
Well, there was a lot of other people, but that was the one
where we knew him from.
Crosby was the one I knew at that time. Yeah, where he was featured.
These were strictly lily-white bands. There wasn't a black musician in the bunch, but they, at times, played very well and very excitingly, and I enjoyed them all.
Perfect. That somehow reminds me of Lizzie Miles, who used to sing up there with Tony Almarico later. Did you ever hear her?

Yeah. I heard Lizzie, oh, a number of times. I don't remember a great deal about her. I kind of liked her. I kind of liked her sometimes. Other times, she was a little bit too much, for my taste, more of a showwoman than a blues singer. And what I was interested in at the time, particularly, was what I thought was pure jazz, whatever that may be. I knew much more what it was then than I do now. Yeah. Yeah. Where was she singing? I don't remember. You might be able to refresh my memory a little, but I don't remember. I don't think I ever heard her with Tony Almarico. I've heard her with other people.
Yeah, well, I just remember that because she was accepted as part of the show with Tony Almarico.
And she was accepted. And there was a Lily White
except for her.
And, of course, Lizzie was not so awfully dark. No,
but she's...
She was obviously black. But she also had, I think, a national reputation of the sort. Mm-hmm. And I think that made it a lot easier.
Mm-hmm.
perhaps it was easier for her to approach it, too.
Mm-hmm. She was not mild-mannered by any means. She's not spoken to me, anyway, feelings about rage, as many people were.

I think so, but at the same time, I think a lot of people in, a lot of black performers were also what they felt realistic Mm-hmm. Oh, yeah. in dealing with this so that they would talk pretty freely to people that they either had some trust for or no fear from.
Mm-hmm.
Or perhaps just not in front of witnesses.
Yeah.
And, uh, this, this was, I think, sort of the early end of a transitional period.
Mm-hmm.

And, uh, I think we were all very different back then. And had some different ideas and a lot of, a lot of discomforts and fears which hang on in some ways now despite the fact that there's no need for it.

Yeah, well, she was offended that she couldn't come to the New Orleans Public Library to hear her old records, which Edmond Suchon had given to the library. I can't remember when that was exactly that I was working on cataloging them. stuff

I'd have to look that up, but she, yeah, that's one of the things. That was in the mid-50s. Yeah, that angered her. Yeah, it would have been mid-50s maybe, maybe 53, 54, something like that. In any case, it angered her a good deal. In any event, you said something about an abortive initial attempts having to do with the Nuance Jazz Club? Were there some other jazz clubs, or did the... Oh, I was...

Was that your attempts to get down from... No, there was a, I'm trying to think of the name of the darn thing, it was a much more pretentious sort of name of a club that was organized about 45 or 46, and I think by Pai Dufour, or at least he had something to do with it, and I can't, I can't think of the name of it, it probably couldn't do it.
Well, I belong to the National Jazz Foundation, and they were helpful to me. Pat Spice, the secretary. That might have been. Yeah, I don't know if you ever went to their office, or...
No, this was, they sort of flowered and whelped it before I came on the scene.

Well, in 45, I used to go up there and I would write a letter, and she answered it and told me the names of a lot of the old-time musicians who were in New Orleans, and like, well, Johnny Saint Cyr and Monk Hazel, which Monk was a particular kind to me. Really? Yeah, I've been, and told me about people like Joe Avery and Wilbur Tillman. I mean, well, there was segregation and everything. It didn't mean that the white musicians didn't listen to the blacks and vice versa. They knew each other, and probably played together more than we would know about. Far back in the 20s, but, and before, I'm sure. That's another whole story that we don't know so much about. But anyway, uh, so you did get down, and uh, where were the Jazz Club meetings held?

You know, I don't remember. Let's see. Well, there were, the first one I went to was in a place, I don't recall, was in some, some nightclub, I believe, but I don't have any recollection of what, where it had been.
I don't know what we were talking about.
We were talking about the first Jazz Club meetings that I went to.
Oh yeah, held in some sort of nightclub or something.
Uh, you know, no, I remember what it was. Are you on again? Yeah. Okay. It was in some kind of recreational building on Jefferson Davis Parkway that the
city owned at the time. That comes back to me now. I totally forgot.

And I don't remember anything about it beyond that, except it was a kind of an organizational meeting, much like dozens of other organizational meetings I've been to since. But apparently it took that time, and I remember Myra Menville, Johnny Wiggs, that's where I first met Johnny. Freddie King. Those are about the only people I remember offhand. I remember meetings in the St. Charles Hotel on Sunday afternoons later on, at which there was some music, which was usually not all that great as far as I was concerned. I didn't understand a lot of what was going on, so it wasn't, it didn't seem quite right, but I never quite knew what it was that wasn't quite right about it. And I think maybe in a way that retarded rather than augmented my interest in jazz.
Uh-huh.
Because I wasn't hearing what I wanted to hear, even though I wasn't quite sure what it was that I wanted to hear, for whatever sense that may make.

Uh-huh. Did you, uh, did we go to many private parties, or did you go to many private parties? I don't think many others. You mean whether there were musicians? Yeah, whether there were musicians, or a jam session?
Oh, uh, not a lot, because I don't know that there were all that many, but certainly I would think three or four a year maybe, which, and I suspect probably a dozen or so altogether.
Uh-huh.
Which was certainly a lot more than I ever had before, or since.

Well, of course, let's see, I can't remember what year you got married. I got married in 52. Yeah. And so, uh, you were just about through with medical school. Yeah, I finished in 52. Yeah. And it seems to me you got married in the spring, or? February. February, or the one I'm going to say. Anyway, but just before...
And then I was out of town.
Yeah, and you were out of town.
From, uh, from July of 52 through June of 53.
Well, you had plenty of time to, uh, and, and, and, I won't say you had plenty of time, you had more time before you were married, and had those responsibilities, and...

I don't know for sure. Yeah. I was, I was in school, or I was, and the summers I was out of town working a good part of the time. Uh, no, I didn't really have large quantities of time to follow around.
Yeah, well, certainly after, after children comes, that ties you down, too. I see. Yeah.
Some, yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Because, uh, I'm just thinking about parties I went to and things, and I can't remember how many of Herbert Otto's parties you went to.

One I remember for sure, and it was, it was a particularly exciting one, because somehow he got part of the George Lewis band there, uh, I think Herb Moran was there, too. Uh-huh. And you were there, don't you remember, wasn't Herb there?
Well, uh, if it's the one I'm thinking about, uh, you know, of course I can't place it, both Talbot and Moran were there, full George Lewis band, Talbot Moran, Burbank, and Bob Matthews.
Why, why Bob Matthews? Why do you include Bob Matthews?
Because he's on the tapes. Oh, is he? Oh. Yeah.
Yeah, I remember the tapes, and I remember the music was fantastic.
Yeah, both Herbert and, and, uh, Bob Greenwood had their tape recorders going. Now that, I don't remember that much about. Yeah.
I don't remember that much about it either, except the music impressed me as being extremely good.
It seemed there were a lot of people there, and I'm having an awfully good time. Yeah. I don't remember any dancing, though there may have been.
There was some dancing.
Yeah. There was, there was some guy named John Myner who took photographs. Years later, I discovered we're at the same party by looking at the photographs.
I don't remember. I see, had Myner Sinski come to town with him? Myner?
I don't think so. Myner?
Right now. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
I don't think so. Bob Greenwood had met her at the, uh, uh, working at, she worked at the Tulane Library.
Oh.
But she came to town.
I see.
And I think that was probably after Bob had gotten his masters and had been away for a year.
Mm-hmm. Stored all kind of things with me, I don't remember what.
But I think mainly books, not his tapes, but his tape machine. He took them with, uh, yeah, I'm sure he did take that.
Yeah, I would like to, I would like to hear those tapes again. I'd like to hear those tapes, period, since I don't think I've ever heard the tapes.
Yeah. Just, just the music at the time. Yeah. Did you save many, uh, anything, you know, printed things like books and magazines?
I, off and on, would, would keep magazines of interest, some books on jazz, occasional clippings.
Mm-hmm.

I've got, oh, probably 15 or 20, uh, business cards of various musicians and bands going back, oh, quite a long while. Uh, I've got a Jolly Roll Martin card or two, whether or not it's, whether or not they are original or not, I have no idea. I suspect the reproductions, but I have no way to find out. And not know that I'm particularly all that interested in doing so.
Yeah, uh, I read the record change. I remember reading that at Orange and Vine sometimes. Yeah. I don't know about it every month. I just read it.

I probably have one or two of them somewhere, and a jazz, oh, a jazz finder, and a couple of old Esquire jazz books from, well, a couple of the 1945. Uh-huh. Uh, one of them being an Armed Services edition. We've got, I think, a, one of, I guess, one of Panacier's books, uh, I think also in an Armed Services edition. Nah, things like that. Just minor memorabilia.
Yeah. Uh, when did you go to Atlanta? 1962. 1962. Did you hear any New Orleans musicians over there?

Preservation Hall band there once, actually, well, with Jim Robinson and Percy Humphries, particularly, which must have been about 1970, 69 or 70, uh, after the Atlanta Jazz Club started, about 70, uh, some musicians came by. Doc Evans was there once.
Uh-huh.
The Turk Murphy band was there once, uh, but no specific New Orleans musicians that I remember.
You just happened to remember Percy and Jim. You knew them before.
Yeah. No, I knew, I knew the Preservation Hall people. I knew all of them. Yeah. Or most of them. I think Manny Sales was, was there at that time. Uh-huh.
Yeah, well, he was somebody, I can't remember whether you knew him before or not.
Yeah, I, I saw him at Preservation Hall back, I think before it was called Preservation Hall, uh, back around 1961, I guess. Yeah. Yeah.
In 162. Yeah, well, it was very, in 162.
And I was very impressed by them. I never did hear as much of them as I wanted to.

Uh-huh. Let's see. Now, uh, when you go out and buy 78s or LPs, you mentioned in particular liking Joe H. Lewis's. Yeah. Did you consider that different from, say, King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band or Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five? Did you consider them part of the same tradition or?
Yeah, I did. I wasn't sure what you meant by different. No, as far as I was concerned.
You categorized it all as one under one name, general name.
Basically, New Orleans, a New Orleans style jazz.
Uh-huh.
Not, certainly not the same, but under the same rubric.
Yeah. You know, people, people say things like, that's contemporary New Orleans style. I mean, what, I'm not, 60s and 50s.
Some people have to put a label on everything. Yeah. And it's okay to put a label on things as long as you recognize that that's all it is.
Yeah, and sometimes things work very different.
Yeah.
I mean, bands do, I believe today, have a different approach from the 20s.
Yeah, there's been a lot of, you know, a lot of feedback, a lot of stuff exchanged among different groups. Some for the better, some for the worse.

There weren't that many people in New Orleans collection records, and I think it's a general route. Not that I knew of. Yeah, that we would categorize it as New Orleans jazz, not traditional, not any other name. And we meant nearly always the black guys when we talked about New Orleans jazz.
Well, you know, this was before there was a really established emphasis on jazz criticism.
Mm-hmm.
We assumed that we knew more than anybody else around was likely to. I'm still not convinced that we didn't.
Yeah, well, I, uh, not either. After all, some of the people who had huge collections also didn't go out and listen to live music.
Right.
Or I'm told that it had depressed him to go to some of these places like Lachim's.
And some people who had huge collections didn't listen to them. Oh, sure. You remember Tom Murray? Yeah. And his collection from which he had been separated for a number of years, I think. Mm-hmm.

Well, I mean, there's all kind of collecting. Yeah. There are people who collect labels, as we used to call those people, label collectors. Mm-hmm. They, uh, they didn't necessarily care about the records, the music on the records.

Of course, I remember one record in particular that disappeared about 1946 or 7. I'm still annoyed about. Must have been a little bit later. Which was a, which was a new copy of McKinney Cotton Pickers record that I had bought new in Shanghai, in 19, in Shanghai, China in 1946. It was the only jazz record they had in the shop. Mm-hmm. They had about 20 or 30 copies of the same record. How and why, I do not know. Oh, no. But somebody ripped it off, which annoyed the hell out of me.
Well, there's nothing like Friends. There are a lot of people who are collectors. Yeah. They just got like Friends.

Uh, did you ever go on Bill Russell's record shop? Yeah. I went to Bill Russell's record shop a number of times, although I think he, I think he came to town, well, probably around 52 or 53 when I was in San Francisco.
I think 54.
Well, perhaps he didn't. Yeah, I think he was. And Bill was always...

sort of constrained and stiff in manner and never was willing to talk a lot that I could get out of them. We were always very awkward with each other. Certainly I thought the records he put out under his label were very interesting and very good. I still have a number of them. And what little I've read of his writings I enjoyed but Bill was always difficult for me to talk to so I just didn't talk to him or he didn't talk to me much or something of the sort. Were there many people in the

shop? Musicians or music lovers? Usually when I went by. But you know you have to test them. Yes, I see something tiny. Yeah, but you know this part of it it doesn't pick up. Right here? Yeah, the very beginning doesn't always pick up. But it's going now. Today is what? Today is the Food. August 3rd, 1978. And we're at 5th at, no I'm getting it wrong, not 15. Our address? 715 St. James. St. James. And I have to get you all to give your names. Your right name. Dine Albert. Herbert Hall. Is that your full name? It says Herbert Hall. Oh yeah, I just...
I don't know. Herb is, it's just Herbert, you know. And no middle name at all, huh? No. You don't use that name? Well I use it in the Union but I don't use it as well.

Okay. Well, it may be one of those French names I can't remember. Yeah, mine is Don Albert Dominique. Yeah. Yeah. Where were you born? Reserve Louis, yeah. And do you mind telling me when? I know it's been a few years ago.
Yeah, March 20th, 1907. Watch it. Okay, well. That's it.
He must have been a child when he was playing with Don. Wait a minute. Wait a minute. Okay. Well, I'll ask Robert.
I don't think Robert can remember that far back.

I see. Anyhow, we were going to talk some. I know most of your life has been covered pretty well in various magazines. Thank you. Everything about where you were born and everything. But I just like to try people's voices out. See if it's picking up and the... We don't need to go into Marshal Lawrence and get Thomas and all that. Right. No. Well, you know about those people. Well, I knew Marshal Lawrence. I even knew Thomas' father. Really? Can you... See? Yeah, sure. Yeah, sure. Yeah, I got an interview with Marshal.
All those country boys knew each other.
Yeah, yeah. And Leroy Robinette is in New Orleans. Yeah. He used to play saxophone. Right. We can continue to talk. Well, and... Why did you join Don's family?

Why? You know, uh... I don't know, for some reason I just felt like I wanted to go. You know, the guys give me a zit off and so more of what was happening, and I was like in Silicon Valley, I mean, Sydney, Desiree in New Orleans, and it wasn't very much happening, so I said I wanted to go down. I was single, you know, in Adventures. Oh, yeah. So I thought I...
Did you play on the rubber boats that much?
No, only on gigs. I played a couple gigs at Sydney on the boat, and that was it. Never just worked, stayed on the boats. Mm-hmm.
Yeah, I was just curious about that. So, yeah, well I'm surprised Sydney wasn't new anymore in New Orleans, but those times come to all bands.
In fact, I wasn't in New Orleans that long, you know. See, I was born in New Zealand, as I said, and when I started playing professionally, I went to Baton Rouge.
Mm-hmm.
And from Baton Rouge I went to New Orleans, that was about two years before I left New Orleans. In fact, I was only in New Orleans about two years before I left.
Who were you with in Baton Rouge?
Oh, that's a good question.
Well, I could ask you about some of the bands. Did you know Kid Victor? That's the band.
Oh. Kid Victor. That's right.
Oh.
Kid Victor.
And did you know John Handy up there?
No, Handy had left that one out.
Oh, I see. And what about Robert?
I know Handy used to come to reserve and play all the time from Baton Rouge, you know.

And what about Robert Thomas, Bob Thomas, was he around Baton Rouge, then? I can't remember. He's a trombone player, you might not remember him at all. No. And Tuts Johnson was there? Tuts Johnson was there at the time. Yeah. But you didn't have him.
And Dines.
Wesley Towns was there at the trumpet club? Yes.
Right. Right.

They were all there at the time. We're talking about Baton Rouge, you know, in different places that he played. Was it about the same as New Orleans up there in Baton Rouge as far as music was concerned? Yes, it's probably the same.
It's probably the same.
Were there big bands there?

No, but they were important. Well, at that time it was considered because it was, let's see, it was two saxes. And they had probably a few guys from Downsville. That's one from the Downsville band. Oh, yeah.

I even knew Freddie Landry from there, he used to play around there. Gosh, what was that band that was so famous for? Um, Dowson, you know, and... Well, it'll come to me after a while. Freddie was one of the... I guess it was Williams.
Yeah, Claiborne Williams.

Claiborne Williams. Claiborne Williams. That's the one I'm trying to think of. Yeah. Well, anyway, so they were smaller than Don's band and... Oh, yes. Oh, yes. And was it any different going from Sidney Desdine to Don? Was it about the same kind of band?
Yes, about the same type of band. Reading band with the three, three reads and you know, the full band. Full band. Full band.
Of that period. Right. What you considered a full band. Well, what instrument did you play with Don's band?
Alto type. Yes, they'd lead alto. Baritone, solos. Sopranos type.
And double-oars, clarinets. He played all of them.
Well, would you play solos on different instruments or just baritones? Just baritones.
Most of baritones.
Yeah.
So, uh...
Ciccatro played the clarinets. Hall played the baritone. Dink Taylor played the alto. Mm-hmm.
Have I had any tel-a-solo's? Very few.
Yeah. I think there's one on riffin'. Was it riffin' and swingin'?

No, rockin' and swingin'. Rockin' and swingin'. Rockin' and swingin', yeah. I think there's one on there. Which sounds like it might be contral. Well, if it was, it was contral because that's the band. Yeah, he's on that. That was the reason they did that. Yeah. Now, uh... How did that work though when you're playing...
In a... Playing baritone and alto and clarinet, did you have to change your style to shift from one

to the other much? You play the same place? Well, the only thing I put on baritone most of the work was... Oh. Well, that's what I'm talking about. Would you play the same licks on baritone that you played on clarinet more or less? Or... Oh, I wouldn't think so because it's a different feel. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
When you feel the instrument, when you pick up the instrument, you feel it, you know, you have a tendency to play it differently, you know.
Well, the reason I was thinking about that, because it struck me in listening to Cottrell's playing, that when he played tenor, it was much like his clarinet.
Well, some of the things you do, you know.
Yeah. Same type of licks, difficult...
But the thing about it, you realize that you can't get over those alto or baritone as fast as you can a clarinet. So, you have to change your style somewhat, you know.
Did you listen to any other baritone players that you liked?
Well, at that time we all were listening. Oh, yeah?
Oh, yeah.
We all were listening. We listened to Duke Allen's name mostly. Oh, I see.
With Conny.
Conny and Bigard and Hodges and those people.

He played his nib to Conny. Anybody ever heard in my life? Yeah, well, I've read it. And you can listen to the album that we had, the Rockin' and Swingin' and the Sheikin', you see the same tonation, the same figures.

Well, that's rated up right there with Conny by some of the critics, you know, in one book. I don't know if you've ever seen it. Not straight melody.

Durny.

you got a weak stand somewhere.
